** explain what these CSP-vulnerable patterns are

Explain what these CSP-vulnerable patterns are. Are the current fixes best practice anyway for userscripts ?
Is it normal that these kind of pages exist where these CSP-vulnerable patterns show up. Why has MusicBrainz choosen to implement it like this ?
What is "// @grant        GM_addStyle" good for

** The two CSP-vulnerable patterns

  Pattern 1: Injected <style> elements
  const style = document.createElement('style');
  style.textContent = `.foo { color: red; }`;
  document.head.appendChild(style);
  CSP's style-src directive governs stylesheets — both <link rel="stylesheet"> and <style> blocks, whether they're present in the original HTML or inserted later by any script. The browser doesn't distinguish "page's own script" from "extension-injected script" here; a <style>
  element is a <style> element. Without 'unsafe-inline', a nonce, or a matching hash in the CSP header, the browser parses the tag, computes zero rules from it, and logs a console warning. Silent from the page's perspective — nothing throws, nothing crashes, the CSS just never
  applies.

  Pattern 2: Inline style="..." HTML attributes
  container.innerHTML = `<div style="display:flex;color:red;">...</div>`;
  This is the same CSP directive, different code path: when the browser's HTML parser encounters a style="" attribute (whether parsed from the original document or from a string assigned to .innerHTML), it's treated as inline CSS and checked against the same style-src policy. No
  unsafe-inline → the attribute is parsed but dropped, and the element falls back to its default UA styling (which is why the settings dialog collapsed into plain stacked <div>s).

  There's a close cousin I also found and fixed: inline event-handler attributes (onfocus="...", onclick="..."). Those are gated by script-src, not style-src, but same mechanism — parsed-from-markup inline JS needs a nonce/hash/unsafe-inline too, and we don't have access to the
  page's per-request nonce (it's generated server-side, one nonce per page load, not discoverable or reusable by us).

  What isn't restricted: element.style.color = 'red' or Object.assign(element.style, {...}). These go through the CSSOM (the JS CSSStyleDeclaration object), not the HTML attribute parser. CSP only inspects markup being parsed — HTML text and <style> text — not runtime property
  mutations, even though the browser will later reflect that mutation back into the style="" attribute if you inspect the live DOM. This is exactly why some of the script's buttons already looked fine before any fix: whoever wrote that code happened to use .style.property =
  value, and it was never CSP-vulnerable to begin with.

  Are the fixes best practice?

  Yes, and for reasons beyond just "it satisfies this one CSP header":

  - GM_addStyle is the Tampermonkey/Greasemonkey-idiomatic way to inject a stylesheet from a userscript. It runs in the extension's privileged context rather than being parsed as page content, so it's exempt from the page's CSP entirely — not just this particular policy, but any
  CSP a site might add later. Using the raw DOM API (createElement('style')) was always somewhat fragile for this exact reason; it just hadn't been tested against a page with a real CSP until now.
  - Class-based CSS over inline attributes is generally better practice regardless of CSP — smaller markup, no duplicated declarations across N instances of the same widget, and it's how the settings dialog's own JSDoc comment (the one I found in showModal) already described the
  intent: "Rows are built as real DOM elements... so display:flex cannot be stripped." The original author clearly knew about the innerHTML-stripping risk for some elements and missed it for others — my fix just closes that gap consistently.
  - CSS :focus over onfocus/onblur attributes is strictly better practice independent of CSP too — it's declarative, doesn't need JS to run first, and doesn't risk XSS if the values were ever attacker-influenced (not the case here, but it's the general reason inline event
  handlers are discouraged).

  So: not workarounds bolted on to dodge a policy, but a shift toward the patterns that were already correct in parts of this codebase.

  Is it normal for CSP to vary by page on the same site?

  Yes, this is common and usually deliberate, though it can also be an artifact of infrastructure rather than a security decision. What I found on musicbrainz.org specifically:

  - /account/* pages are served directly by the Perl/Catalyst backend (Plack::Handler::Starlet) and carry the CSP header.
  - General content pages (/artist/..., /release-group/..., /search) are served through an edge/cache layer (openresty) and carry no CSP header at all.

  Two plausible explanations, and they're not mutually exclusive:

  1. Deliberate, risk-tiered hardening. /account/* is where session cookies, OAuth app tokens, and (as of the change that started this investigation) digest-auth credentials and CSRF tokens live. It's standard practice to apply a stricter CSP to authentication/account-management
  surfaces first — they're the highest-value XSS target — even when the rest of the site hasn't been migrated yet. A strict style-src/script-src with nonces meaningfully raises the bar against injected-script and injected-style attacks on exactly the pages where credential theft
  would matter most.
  2. Infrastructure boundary, not a security choice per se. The openresty-fronted content pages may simply not have been routed through whatever middleware sets the CSP header — CSP might be rolling out incrementally as MusicBrainz migrates parts of the stack, or the cache layer
  strips response headers it doesn't know about. Under this reading, "no CSP on content pages" isn't a statement that those pages are less important, just that CSP hasn't reached them yet.

  Given the new digest-auth feature (password-adjacent, MD5-hash-based legacy auth) landed on /account/applications around the same time you noticed the breakage, my best guess is the CSP tightening is part of the same security push — plausibly rolled out to /account/* first
  precisely because that's where a new credential-handling feature just went in. I don't have visibility into MusicBrainz's actual deployment history to confirm which of the two explanations is right, though.

  What does // @grant GM_addStyle actually do

  @grant lines declare which privileged Tampermonkey APIs (GM_* functions) a script is allowed to call. Tampermonkey builds a sandboxed execution environment per script; only the specific GM_* functions you list are exposed into that sandbox (this is also a security boundary —
  it's why a userscript can't silently start doing GM_xmlhttpRequest to exfiltrate data unless it explicitly declared that grant, so a user reviewing the script's permissions before installing can see what it's allowed to touch).

  Without @grant GM_addStyle, the function simply doesn't exist in that script's global scope — calling it throws GM_addStyle is not defined, not a CSP error. That's why I had to add the grant to both ShowAllEntityData.user.js/VZ_MBLibrary.user.js and separately to
  MB_PageEnhancer.user.js: @required library code executes inside the sandbox of whichever top-level script pulled it in, so each consumer needs its own grant declared, even though the library only has one copy of the code that calls GM_addStyle.

  Functionally, GM_addStyle(css) creates a <style> element and inserts it into <head> — same end result as the manual createElement/appendChild pattern — but because it goes through Tampermonkey's privileged injection path rather than the page's own DOM-manipulation API as seen
  by CSP, the browser doesn't treat it as page-authored content subject to the page's style-src policy.

** what does CSP stands for and how it is declared in a web page

 What CSP stands for

  Content Security Policy — an HTTP response header (or an equivalent <meta> tag) that lets a website tell the browser "only trust content from these sources; refuse everything else," as a defense mostly against XSS and data-injection attacks. Instead of trying to sanitize every
  possible injection point in the app, the site declares an allowlist once and the browser enforces it uniformly — even against content the site's own server-side code might accidentally have failed to escape.

  How it's declared

  1. HTTP response header (the way MusicBrainz does it — what I saw via curl -I):
  Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-JexaXHNPXIhsWLOJi4KyNC0-cQ39sonkkOEkwEYkxTk' staticbrainz.org static.metabrainz.org; style-src 'self' staticbrainz.org static.metabrainz.org; img-src 'self' data: staticbrainz.org
  static.metabrainz.org; frame-src 'self'
  Set server-side, applies to the whole document as soon as the response arrives — before the browser even starts parsing the HTML body. This is the more common and more robust mechanism, since it can't be tampered with by anything running in the page (a <meta> tag injected via
  XSS could theoretically be neutralized or overridden by later markup).

  2. HTML <meta> tag, as an alternative when you don't control server headers:
  <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src 'self'; style-src 'self'">
  Same syntax as the header value, just delivered in-document. Weaker in a few ways: it only takes effect once the parser reaches that <meta> tag (so anything earlier in <head> is unprotected), and it can't set a few directives at all (frame-ancestors, report-uri/report-to, and
  the sandboxing directives require the HTTP header form).

  Reading the directive syntax

  Each directive is name value1 value2 ..., directives separated by ;:

  ┌─────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │    Directive    │                                                      Governs                                                       │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ default-src     │ Fallback for any directive not explicitly listed                                                                   │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ script-src      │ JavaScript sources — <script> tags, inline scripts, eval                                                           │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ style-src       │ CSS sources — <style> tags, <link rel=stylesheet>, inline style="" attributes (the one that broke this userscript) │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ img-src         │ Image sources                                                                                                      │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ frame-src       │ What can be embedded in an <iframe> on this page                                                                   │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ frame-ancestors │ What sites are allowed to embed this page in their own <iframe> (clickjacking defense)                             │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ connect-src     │ fetch/XHR/WebSocket targets                                                                                        │
  └─────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Common source-value keywords: 'self' (same origin), 'none' (nothing), a bare hostname like staticbrainz.org (that origin, any scheme/port unless specified), 'unsafe-inline' (allow inline script/style — the escape hatch that's absent here), 'nonce-<random>' (a one-time token the
  server prints fresh into both the header and the specific <script>/<style> tags it wants to allow, so only server-generated tags — never attacker- or extension-injected ones — can match), and 'sha256-<hash>' (allow a specific inline script/style block by its exact content
  hash, used the same way as a nonce but for static, unchanging inline blocks).

  That 'nonce-JexaXHNPXIhsWLOJi4KyNC0-cQ39sonkkOEkwEYkxTk' in MusicBrainz's script-src is exactly this mechanism — it changes on every single page load, which is precisely why a userscript can never legitimately obtain it and use it to smuggle its own <script>/<style> past the
  policy. GM_addStyle sidesteps the whole problem instead of trying to solve it: it doesn't add page-authored content at all, it injects through the browser extension's own privileged API, which CSP has no visibility into.

** is it possible for musicbrainz to actually break my userscript completely

● Short answer: no, not completely — but it's worth understanding precisely why, and where the real risk actually is (spoiler: it's not CSP).

  Why CSP can't stop the script from running

  Tampermonkey userscripts execute in what browsers call an "isolated world" — the same underlying browser extension mechanism as Chrome/Firefox extension content scripts. This is a fundamental part of the extension security model, not something MusicBrainz's server can see or
  influence: the page's CSP governs content the page itself is responsible for (its own <script> tags, inline handlers, stylesheets, images, fetches made through the page's own APIs). A userscript's own JS execution, DOM reads, and any GM_* API calls sit outside that boundary
  entirely. MusicBrainz cannot write a CSP header that says "block Tampermonkey scripts" — CSP has no vocabulary for that, and even if it did, the isolated-world architecture means the browser wouldn't apply it there.

  That's also why GM_addStyle works as a fix at all: it's not a clever workaround exploiting a loophole, it's the intended, documented mechanism for exactly this situation — Tampermonkey deliberately provides privileged APIs (GM_addStyle, GM_xmlhttpRequest, GM_setValue, etc.)
  specifically so script authors don't have to fight the page's CSP for legitimate extension behavior.

  What CSP genuinely CAN keep breaking

  Only the parts of the script that manipulate the DOM the same way the page itself would — using standard web-platform APIs instead of GM_* equivalents:

  - document.createElement('style') / inline style="" — what we just fixed, twice over
  - Any inline event-handler attribute built via innerHTML (the onfocus/onblur case)
  - If the script ever used the page's own fetch()/XMLHttpRequest instead of GM_xmlhttpRequest — it already correctly uses GM_xmlhttpRequest (see the @connect directives), so this is a non-issue
  - Injecting <script> tags into the page DOM to run page-context code — the script doesn't do this anywhere I've seen
  - If MusicBrainz added img-src restrictions that somehow applied to elements the script injects — currently CAA/EAA thumbnails etc. are just <img> elements the extension DOM API creates, which (like style attributes) is markup subject to CSP if img-src were tightened without a
  matching allowance

  So: CSP getting stricter could keep chipping away at cosmetic/DOM-injection details, the same category of bug as the last two sessions. It's annoying and needs periodic fixing, but it degrades gracefully — features go unstyled or slightly broken, not "the whole script stops
  running."

  The actually bigger risk: MusicBrainz restructuring the DOM

  Looking at debug/NOTES.md's history, essentially every prior "page type broken" bug in this project has been MusicBrainz changing HTML structure — new sections, renamed classes, moved elements, added/removed wrapper divs — not CSP. That risk is unrelated to security headers
  entirely and is the one that can genuinely break a feature completely: if pageDefinitions' matchers, parseDocumentForTables, or a column extractor's selectors no longer match the real DOM, that feature silently does nothing or throws, with no graceful degradation. That's a
  structural coupling the script has always had with MusicBrainz's markup and always will — CSP is a comparatively narrow, newer, and more cosmetic risk by comparison.

  One honest caveat

  There's a genuinely murkier CSP directive called require-trusted-types-for 'script' (Trusted Types) that restricts DOM XSS sinks like innerHTML at a lower level than style-src/script-src. Whether that would affect extension-injected innerHTML writes depends on
  browser/version-specific implementation details I'm not fully certain of — it's rarer, MusicBrainz doesn't currently use it, and I wouldn't want to overstate my confidence either way. If they ever adopted it, it could plausibly force a deeper rewrite (buildling everything via
  createElement/textContent instead of innerHTML strings) — but that's speculative, not something currently in play.

* DONE flags - refactoring

#+begin_example
     * Non-flag (Locality/Region) links are positional, not semantic: the
     * FIRST one seen (per `areaState.count === 0`) is the most specific
     * (Locality — e.g. city/neighbourhood); every subsequent one is broader
     * (Region — e.g. county/state, comma-joined). MusicBrainz area links
     * carry no type information, and the chain depth varies per place rather
     * than per country, so position is the only signal available — EXCEPT
     * when that first link itself carries a subdivision-flag icon (meaning no
     * city/locality was ever entered, only a bare state/province) AND the
     * row's country is in the internal `AREA_FLAG_REGION_COUNTRIES`
     * list: that link is then forced into Region instead, since it's
     * conceptually a Region-level entity even though it's positionally first.
#+end_example

Why is the "Relationships" column missing on the final rendered page:

Only analyze, do not code anything

#+begin_example
● Root cause: injectedColumns is nested one level too shallow

  In your edit:

  features: {
      collapsableColumns: [ 'Authors', 'Recording artists', 'Other artists', 'ISWC', 'Lyrics languages', 'Attributes' ],
      extractMainColumn: 'Work',
      stickyColumn: 'Work'
  },
  injectedColumns: [ 'Relationships' ],   // ← sibling of `features`, not inside it
  tableMode: 'single'

  injectedColumns sits as a sibling of features on the page-definition object, but every consumer in the script reads it as def.features.injectedColumns. There is no code path anywhere in the file that reads a
  top-level def.injectedColumns — I grepped for it and confirmed all ~60 existing correct usages nest it inside features: { … } (e.g. line 6853), and the two builder functions that actually turn the
  declaration into runtime state both do def?.features?.injectedColumns:

  - buildActiveInjectedColumns(def) — line 4139-4141
  - buildActiveReleaseEventColumns(def) — line 4106-4108

  With the key outside features, def.features.injectedColumns is undefined, so buildActiveInjectedColumns() returns []. That has two concrete effects downstream:

  1. Header never created: the header-injection block (line 28815, if (activeInjectedColumns.length) { … }) never runs, so no <th>Relationships</th> is added to theadRow.
  2. Fetch never runs: initRelationshipsColumn() — the function that does the actual WS2 inc=url-rels+artist-rels fetch and populates the column — is only ever invoked from if (activeInjectedColumns.length)
  initRelationshipsColumn(); (lines 31774 and 44253). With an empty array, it's simply never called.

  So there is no bug in the extraction/render pipeline itself — the feature is just never activated, because the declaration lives in a place nothing reads.

  Why the debug HTML makes it look worse than it is (a red herring)

  The <td class="relationships"> cell you see in debug/work-rel.html (with the secondhandsongs/wikidata favicon links) is not MusicBrainz data and not this script's own Relationships feature — it's clutter
  injected by the separately-installed "jesus2099 mb. SUPER MIND CONTROL" userscript. This script already has dedicated, unconditional cleanup for exactly that class (see the 'jesus2099' columnEraser and
  _watchForLateJesus2099Injections()'s _stripRelationshipsTd, lines ~32075-32134, and the accompanying JSDoc explicitly calling out <td class="relationships"> as "jesus2099's own class, distinct from this
  script's own .mb-rel-cell"). That cell gets stripped as clutter regardless of your page-definition change — its disappearance between work-rel.html and work-rel-bug.html is by design and has nothing to do
  with injectedColumns.

  That's also why the column count in debug/work-rel-bug.html still comes out to 11, same as the original — masking the bug if you just eyeball "did a column disappear": the jesus2099 cell (-1) and the
  merge-checkbox column (-1) are correctly dropped, while extractMainColumn: 'Work' correctly adds its own two synthetic columns, MB-Name and Comment (+2). Those four unrelated, expected changes happen to net
  to zero, so the real missing column (the genuine, WS2-populated "Relationships" column your edit was meant to enable) doesn't show up as a numeric shortfall — it's just silently never created at all.

  Fix would be: move injectedColumns: [ 'Relationships' ] inside the features: { … } object, alongside collapsableColumns/extractMainColumn/stickyColumn (not applying this now, per your request).
#+end_example

#+begin_example
● Root cause: _suppressRelationshipsIfNoReleaseOrReleaseGroupLinks() strips the header, but runs before the data cells even exist

  For tableMode: 'single' pages, the render sequence (in the else branch after renderFinalTable(allRows), lines 31505-31534) is:

  await renderFinalTable(allRows);
  document.querySelectorAll('table.tbl thead').forEach(cleanupHeaders);   // (1) creates <th>Relationships</th>
  ...
  if (mainTable) _suppressRelationshipsIfNoReleaseOrReleaseGroupLinks(mainTable);  // (2) removes it again
  ...
  if (activeInjectedColumns.length) initRelationshipsColumn();            // (3) creates + fills .mb-rel-cell <td>s

  Step 1 — cleanupHeaders() (line 28585) sees activeInjectedColumns is now correctly populated (since you moved the key inside features) and appends a <th data-col-name="Relationships"
  class="mb-injected-column"> to the header row.

  Step 2 — _suppressRelationshipsIfNoReleaseOrReleaseGroupLinks(mainTable) (line 42183) runs immediately after. Its whole premise (per its own JSDoc, lines 42150-42176) is built for pages like
  artist-relationships/label-relationships/place-performances, where each row's "Title" cell links to a /release/… or /release-group/… page and the injected Relationships column shows that release's
  relationships — so a sub-section with no release/release-group link genuinely has nothing useful to show. It checks:

  const _hasLink = !!table.querySelector(
      'tbody td:not(.mb-sticky-col):not(.mb-rel-cell) a[href*="/release/"],' +
      'tbody td:not(.mb-sticky-col):not(.mb-rel-cell) a[href*="/release-group/"]'
  );
  if (_hasLink) return; // leave table untouched
  // ...otherwise remove the "Relationships" <th> and any .mb-rel-cell <td>s

  On artist-works, every row's main link is /work/<mbid> (excluded anyway via :not(.mb-sticky-col)) and the other cells link to /artist/… (Authors/Recording artists) — there is no /release/ or /release-group/
  link anywhere in the table, because a Work simply isn't a release. So _hasLink is always false here, and the function unconditionally deletes the header cell it just gained in step 1.

  Step 3 — initRelationshipsColumn() runs later still (line 31774/42680). It doesn't know or care that the header was already removed — its own _ensureRelCell() helper (line 42702) just row.appendChild()s a
  td.mb-rel-cell to every row regardless, then fills it with the fetched WS2 relationship icons (for artist-works, entityType: 'work', inc: url-rels + artist-rels — i.e. exactly the kind of external-link
  icons, secondhandsongs/wikidata, that jesus2099 was faking in the native page).

  Net effect: you get a real, correctly-populated data column appended as the last <td> of every row, but with no <th> above it — because step 2's guard, designed around "is this row about a
  release/release-group," fired on a page type it was never meant to apply to, and deleted the header before step 3 ever created the data it belongs to.
#+end_example

what would be the fix to make this work also on artist-works pageTypes, as the relationships actually exist there ? do not code just show the solution

#+begin_example
● The fix: gate the suppression guard on entityType, not just link presence

  The guard _suppressRelationshipsIfNoReleaseOrReleaseGroupLinks() is only valid for page types where the Relationships column targets a release or release-group entity discovered via a link in the row —
  that's true for entityType: 'release' (the default branch — artist-relationships, label-relationships, place-performances, releasegroup-releases, recording-releases, etc.) and entityType: 'release-group'
  (artist-releasegroups, whose Title links to /release-group/…, which the existing _hasLink check already matches).

  It is not valid for entityType: 'work' (artist-works only, per buildActiveInjectedColumns(), line 4139-4158): there the column fetches the row's own Work's relationships via its own MBID — there's no
  release/release-group link to check for in the first place, so "no release link found" is not evidence of "nothing to show" the way it is for the other page types.

  Since activeInjectedColumns[0].entityType already carries exactly this distinction (it's the same field initRelationshipsColumn() reads to build its WS2 request), the fix is a single early-return added right
  after the existing activeInjectedColumns.length check in _suppressRelationshipsIfNoReleaseOrReleaseGroupLinks() (line 42183-42185):

  function _suppressRelationshipsIfNoReleaseOrReleaseGroupLinks(table) {
      if (!table) return;
      if (!activeInjectedColumns.length) return; // Relationships not active for this pageType

      // This guard's premise (no /release/ or /release-group/ link ⇒ nothing to
      // show) only applies when the injected Relationships column targets a
      // release/release-group entity discovered via a link in the row (entityType
      // 'release' or 'release-group'). On artist-works (entityType 'work') the
      // column targets the row's OWN Work entity via its own MBID — there's no
      // release/release-group link to find here by design, so the check must not
      // gate the column for that entityType.
      if (activeInjectedColumns[0].entityType === 'work') return;

      // ...rest of the function unchanged...

  That's the whole fix: one guard clause, keyed off data the function already has access to. It doesn't touch cleanupHeaders(), initRelationshipsColumn(), or the header-injection logic at all — those are
  already correct once the misplaced-key issue is fixed. It also doesn't affect any other page type, since every other page type currently in pageDefinitions resolves to entityType: 'release' or
  'release-group', both of which keep going through the existing link-check logic exactly as before.
#+end_example

why are the 'Release country' and 'Release date' columns still not rendered in collapsable mode, alos they have multi-row cells

#+begin_example
● Root cause: a missing initCollapsableColumns() re-run after the third population pass

  The three columns are populated in three separate, sequential passes inside initReleaseEventsColumn() (line 41895), and initCollapsableColumns() only gets re-invoked after the first two of them — not the
  third, which is the one that actually fills "Release country" and "Release date".

  Pass 1 — initial render. When the table is first built, "Release events" is a bare placeholder td.mb-re-cell and "Release country"/"Release date" are bare placeholder td.mb-ice-cells (see _ensureIceCells,
  line 42038) — all empty. initCollapsableColumns() runs once here (as part of the normal render pipeline) and finds 0 <ul><li> items in any of the three, so no toggle is installed for any of them. This is
  expected and harmless on its own.

  Pass 2 — initReleaseEventsColumn() fetches and populates "Release events". It fetches WS2 data, calls _rePopulateCell() to fill each td.mb-re-cell with a real <ul><li> list, and then explicitly re-runs
  collapsable-column detection:

  // line 41978-41982
  // Re-run initCollapsableColumns: it ran before cells were populated so
  // found 0 ul>li items. Now that cells have real content, install toggles.
  if (activeReleaseEventColumns.length) {
      document.querySelectorAll('table.tbl').forEach(t => initCollapsableColumns(t));
  }

  At this point "Release events" now has content, so it correctly gets its collapse toggle. But "Release country"/"Release date" are still empty placeholders — the extractor that fills them hasn't run yet.

  Pass 3 — applyInjectedColumnExtractors(), called immediately after. This is the function (line 42014-42148) that actually runs SyntheticColumnDataExtractor.splitCountryDate against the now-populated "Release
  events" cell and fills the "Release country"/"Release date" td.mb-ice-cell placeholders with their own parallel <ul><li> structures (confirmed in the extractor's own JSDoc at line 3899-3925: "For
  multi-event cells each <li> produces one parallel <li> in the two output cells"). So yes — these two columns genuinely do end up holding real multi-row list content, exactly as you observed.

  The problem: nothing calls initCollapsableColumns() again after this third pass. I checked — applyInjectedColumnExtractors()'s entire body (lines 42014-42148) never calls it, and it has exactly one call site
  in the whole file (line 41985), always immediately after the pass-2 re-run at line 41981, never before or after it a second time. So by the time "Release country"/"Release date" actually receive their
  multi-row content, the one-shot collapsable-column scan that would have noticed them has already run and moved on — permanently.

  Why "Release events" alone worked before your change: it's the only column whose population is directly followed by an initCollapsableColumns() re-run. Adding "Release country"/"Release date" to
  collapsableColumns was the logically correct thing to do — initCollapsableColumns() does look for those names too — but their data simply never exists yet at either of the two moments that function is
  actually invoked in the render sequence for this page type.
#+end_example

<p><bdi><b>Bruce Frederick Joseph Springsteen</b> (born September 23, 1949) is an American singer, songwriter, and musician. Nicknamed "the Boss", Springsteen has released 21 studio albums spanning six decades; most feature the E Street Band, his backing band since 1972.
</bdi></p><p><bdi>Springsteen released his first two albums, <i>Greetings from Asbury Park, N.J.</i> and <i>The Wild, the Innocent &amp; the E Street Shuffle</i>, in 1973. He achieved worldwide popularity with <i>Born to Run</i> (1975). He followed with <i>Darkness on the Edge of Town</i> (1978) and <i>The River</i> (1980), Springsteen's first album to top the <i>Billboard</i> 200 chart. After releasing the solo acoustic album <i>Nebraska</i> (1982), he recorded <i>Born in the U.S.A.</i> (1984) with the E Street Band. It is his most successful album and one of the best-selling albums of all time. Springsteen mostly hired session musicians for his next three albums, <i>Tunnel of Love</i> (1987), <i>Human Touch</i> (1992), and <i>Lucky Town</i> (1992). He reassembled the E Street Band for <i>Greatest Hits</i> (1995), and recorded the acoustic album <i>The Ghost of Tom Joad</i> (1995) and the EP <i>Blood Brothers</i> (1996) solo.
</bdi></p><p><bdi>Following the Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band Reunion Tour in 1999 and 2000, Springsteen released <i>The Rising</i> (2002), dedicated to the victims of the September 11 attacks. This was followed by two folk albums, <i>Devils &amp; Dust</i> (2005) and <i>We Shall Overcome: The Seeger Sessions</i> (2006), his first cover album. Springsteen followed with <i>Magic</i> (2007), <i>Working on a Dream</i> (2009), <i>Wrecking Ball</i> (2012), and <i>High Hopes</i> (2014). In 2017, 2018, and 2021, Springsteen performed <i>Springsteen on Broadway</i>, performing songs and telling stories from his 2016 autobiography. He released the solo album <i>Western Stars</i> in 2019, <i>Letter to You</i> with the E Street Band in 2020, and a solo cover album, <i>Only the Strong Survive</i>, in 2022. With <i>Letter to You</i>, Springsteen became the first artist to release a top-five album in six consecutive decades. He released the politically charged "Streets of Minneapolis" in 2026, which reached number one on the iTunes Top Songs chart.
</bdi></p><p><bdi>A prominent musician from the album era, Springsteen has sold more than 140 million records worldwide, making him one of the best-selling music artists of all time. His accolades include 20 Grammy Awards, two Golden Globes, an Academy Award, and a Special Tony Award. He was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1999, received the Kennedy Center Honors in 2009, was named MusiCares person of the year in 2013, and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016 and the National Medal of Arts in 2023. In 2010, <i>Rolling Stone</i> ranked Springsteen 23rd on its list of the "100 Greatest Artists of All Time", describing him as "the embodiment of rock and roll". In 2025, Springsteen became one of only five artists to gross over $2.3 billion in touring thanks to his 2023–2025 Tour with the E Street Band.
</bdi></p></div><p style=""><a class="wikipedia-extract-toggle" href="#">Show more...</a></p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Springsteen" style="">Continue reading at Wikipedia...</a> <small style="">Wikipedia content provided under the terms of the <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/">Creative Commons BY-SA license</a></small><h2 class="annotation mb-h2-processed mb-toggle-h2" title="Click to collapse/uncollapse section (Ctrl+Click to toggle ALL sections)" style="cursor: pointer; class="annotation"></div><script type="application/json">{"cachedWikipediaExtract":{"content":"<p class=\"mw-empty-elt\">\n\n<\/bdi><\/p>\n\n<p><bdi><b>Bruce Frederick Joseph Springsteen<\/b> (born September 23, 1949) is an American singer, songwriter, and musician. Nicknamed \"the Boss\", Springsteen has released 21 studio albums spanning six decades; most feature the E Street Band, his backing band since 1972.\n<\/bdi><\/p><p><bdi>Springsteen released his first two albums, <i>Greetings from Asbury Park, N.J.<\/i> and <i>The Wild, the Innocent &amp; the E Street Shuffle<\/i>, in 1973. He achieved worldwide popularity with <i>Born to Run<\/i> (1975). He followed with <i>Darkness on the Edge of Town<\/i> (1978) and <i>The River<\/i> (1980), Springsteen's first album to top the <i>Billboard<\/i> 200 chart. After releasing the solo acoustic album <i>Nebraska<\/i> (1982), he recorded <i>Born in the U.S.A.<\/i> (1984) with the E Street Band. It is his most successful album and one of the best-selling albums of all time. Springsteen mostly hired session musicians for his next three albums, <i>Tunnel of Love<\/i> (1987), <i>Human Touch<\/i> (1992), and <i>Lucky Town<\/i> (1992). He reassembled the E Street Band for <i>Greatest Hits<\/i> (1995), and recorded the acoustic album <i>The Ghost of Tom Joad<\/i> (1995) and the EP <i>Blood Brothers<\/i> (1996) solo.\n<\/bdi><\/p><p><bdi>Following the Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band Reunion Tour in 1999 and 2000, Springsteen released <i>The Rising<\/i> (2002), dedicated to the victims of the September 11 attacks. This was followed by two folk albums, <i>Devils &amp; Dust<\/i> (2005) and <i>We Shall Overcome: The Seeger Sessions<\/i> (2006), his first cover album. Springsteen followed with <i>Magic<\/i> (2007), <i>Working on a Dream<\/i> (2009), <i>Wrecking Ball<\/i> (2012), and <i>High Hopes<\/i> (2014). In 2017, 2018, and 2021, Springsteen performed <i>Springsteen on Broadway<\/i>, performing songs and telling stories from his 2016 autobiography. He released the solo album <i>Western Stars<\/i> in 2019, <i>Letter to You<\/i> with the E Street Band in 2020, and a solo cover album, <i>Only the Strong Survive<\/i>, in 2022. With <i>Letter to You<\/i>, Springsteen became the first artist to release a top-five album in six consecutive decades. He released the politically charged \"Streets of Minneapolis\" in 2026, which reached number one on the iTunes Top Songs chart.\n<\/bdi><\/p><p><bdi>A prominent musician from the album era, Springsteen has sold more than 140 million records worldwide, making him one of the best-selling music artists of all time. His accolades include 20 Grammy Awards, two Golden Globes, an Academy Award, and a Special Tony Award. He was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1999, received the Kennedy Center Honors in 2009, was named MusiCares person of the year in 2013, and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016 and the National Medal of Arts in 2023. In 2010, <i>Rolling Stone<\/i> ranked Springsteen 23rd on its list of the \"100 Greatest Artists of All Time\", describing him as \"the embodiment of rock and roll\". In 2025, Springsteen became one of only five artists to gross over $2.3 billion in touring thanks to his 2023–2025 Tour with the E Street Band.\n<\/bdi><\/p>","language":"en","canonical":"Bruce Springsteen","title":"Bruce Springsteen","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Springsteen"},"entity":{"entityType":"artist","gid":"70248960-cb53-4ea4-943a-edb18f7d336f"}}</script><div ● No, no change needed there.

  BruceBaseParser.user.js already has // @grant GM_addStyle (line 24) and already calls GM_addStyle(...) directly (line 11879) — it didn't need this grant added, unlike MB_PageEnhancer which was missing it before the CSP fix. It also:

  - @requires VZ_MBLibrary.user.js via a local file:///… path, so it always picks up whatever's currently on disk — no pinned/cached version to bump.
  - Doesn't reference LIBRARY_VERSION or hardcode any VZ_MBLibrary version string anywhere in its code.

  So the 3.19.0 → 3.19.1 library bump requires no change in BruceBaseParser.user.js.



* Performance fixes — ready to implement (analysed, approach agreed)

# Current work

## Performance fixes — ready to implement (analysed, approach agreed)

### P1 — Filter performance (do in order, each builds on previous)
- Fix A: test-before-clone — reverse map/filter order in runFilter(),
  separate highlight from match in testRowMatch()
- Fix B: pre-cache extracted text — WeakMap keyed on source rows,
  populated at render time, invalidated on new fetch
- Pattern 2: two-phase matching — cheap global string.includes first,
  expensive querySelector/regexp only on survivors
- Pattern 3: adaptive debounce — scale delay to row count, user setting
  becomes a floor not an override
- Pattern 1: incremental filter — on query extension test only previous
  match set, not all rows; invalidate on sort/fetch/settings change
- Fix C: display:none instead of re-render — keep all rows in DOM,
  toggle visibility; eliminates DOM rebuild + all post-render hooks
  from filter path; bigbox rebuild becomes one-time not per-keystroke
- Pattern 4: rAF chunked render — abort token pattern; post-render
  hooks only fire for completed render not abandoned ones
- Pattern 5: Intersection Observer for CAA — lazy-load art as cells
  scroll into viewport; guard with row-count threshold setting
- Pattern 6: result cache — Map keyed on normalised query, max 50
  entries, evict oldest; invalidate on fetch/sort/settings change

### P2 — Relationship column correctness bug
Three-part fix (race condition between fetch queue and runFilter DOM rebuild):
1. After renderFinalTable/renderGroupedTable in runFilter: call
   initRelationshipsColumn() if any td.mb-rel-cell[data-rel-done!="1"] exist
2. Sync source rows immediately in _populateCells after each MBID
   completes — not only in queue.then()
3. queue.then() bulk sync becomes safety net, skip already-synced cells

### P3 — Column resize progress indicator + Chrome unresponsive dialog fix
- Make toggleAutoResizeColumns() async
- Show same overlay as renderRowsChunked (📐 Measuring column widths…)
- Chunk inner row measurement loop at 100 rows, yield between chunks
- Disable resize button during operation, re-enable in finally block
- await call site

## Expected gains (5000 row table)
- Filter: 1200–2200ms → 15–30ms per keystroke (50–80× for chars 2+)
- Resize: Chrome unresponsive dialog eliminated entirely
- Relationship column: empty cells self-heal after filter, no manual retry

## Notes
- Fix A+B+Pattern 2 first — confirm working before proceeding
- Fix C changes the render model — test all post-render features after
- CAA bigbox _artInitBigPics synchronous DOM loop is the non-network
  cost per keystroke; Fix C eliminates it automatically
- Relationship fetching itself is async and causes no UI lag —
  the bug is correctness only, not performance
- Do NOT add renameH2ToH3 or insertH2 to user-tags definition
  (see CLAUDE.md — container re-root fix handles it correctly)

Yes, all three are fully independent. They touch completely different code paths:
P3 (resize) — toggleAutoResizeColumns() only. No shared state with anything else. Completely self-contained. Lowest risk, do this first — it's also the simplest and gives you immediate visible proof it works (no more Chrome dialog).
P2 (relationship correctness) — initRelationshipsColumn(), _populateCells(), and a small addition to runFilter()'s post-render hook block. The runFilter touch is additive only (one if block at the end) — it doesn't change any existing filter logic.
P1 (filter performance) — runFilter(), testRowMatch(), renderRowsChunked(), and new infrastructure (WeakMap cache, _filterResultCache, _lastMatchingIndices, abort token). The largest change surface of the three.
Within P1 the sub-fixes are also independent of each other — but not equally safe to reorder:

Recommended session order:
Session 1: P3 (resize)         — 30 min, immediate proof of value
Session 2: P2 (relationship)   — 45 min, correctness fix
Session 3: P1 Fix A+B+Pattern2 — 60 min, confirm before proceeding
Session 4: P1 Pattern 3+6      — 20 min, trivial additions
Session 5: P1 Pattern 1+Fix C  — 60 min, biggest architectural change
Session 6: P1 Pattern 4+5      — 45 min, polish
Each session ends with a working, tested, committed state. If any session produces a regression you git checkout -- . and lose nothing.

* question about ordering
** initial

I implemented:

- Fix A+B+Pattern2
- Pattern 3+6

Is it safe to apply the fix "Abort token in renderRowsChunked / renderGroupedTable" next

and later

the three targeted changes:

1. _updateAllColHeaderCounts — defer or cache
2. initCollapsableColumns cleanup passes — consolidate into one scan
3. initCollapsableColumns per-column body scans — single shared scan

and finally finish of with

- Pattern 1+Fix C
- Pattern 4+5

** answer

Yes, that ordering is safe. Let me go through each transition:

Abort token → safe to do next
It's purely additive to renderGroupedTable and renderRowsChunked — a counter increment at the start, a guard check at each yield point. It doesn't touch the match logic, the clone path, the highlight path, or any post-render hook. Fix A+B are already in place so the render is faster, but the abort token is needed regardless — it fixes the correctness bug (concurrent renders) independently of performance.
One thing to verify after implementing: confirm the post-render hooks (initCaaPics, initRelationshipsColumn, makeH2sCollapsible, etc.) are inside the generation guard so they only fire for the winning render, not for abandoned ones.

initCollapsableColumns fixes → safe after abort token
The three targeted changes are purely internal refactoring of initCollapsableColumns and _updateAllColHeaderCounts. They don't interact with the abort token, the clone pipeline, or Fix A+B+Pattern2 in any way. The deferred _updateAllColHeaderCounts is the highest-value change here — wrapping it in setTimeout(0) immediately removes the dominant post-render freeze on large tables without touching any logic.
One dependency to be aware of: _updateAllColHeaderCounts deferred via setTimeout(0) means the unique-value counts in column headers appear slightly after render completes rather than simultaneously. This is purely cosmetic and correct behaviour — just verify the status display timing still reads sensibly.

Pattern 1 + Fix C → safe after initCollapsableColumns fixes
This is the right time for Fix C because:

Fix C (display:none) keeps all rows in the DOM — initCollapsableColumns must work correctly on the full row set, not just visible rows. The initCollapsableColumns fixes ensure it's fast enough to run once at initial render without freezing. If Fix C had been applied before the initCollapsableColumns fixes, you'd have a fast filter but a slow initial render with a potential Chrome dialog.
Pattern 1 (incremental filter) depends on Fix B (text cache) being in place, which it is. It also pairs naturally with Fix C since both assume the match set is maintained as state rather than recomputed from scratch.

One thing to audit before implementing Fix C: every post-render hook that currently runs inside runFilter's render path needs to be reviewed — some can be skipped entirely (DOM is stable, hooks already ran at initial render), others need an in-place update path instead of a full re-run. Specifically:

initCollapsableColumns — skip on filter (rows already have toggles from initial render)
initCaaPics/initEaaPics — skip on filter (visibility toggle doesn't affect already-initialised art cells)
initRelationshipsColumn — skip on filter (correctness fix from P2 handles this separately)
highlightText — needs in-place update on source rows (the main new work for Fix C)
updateH2Count — still needed, reads visible row count


Pattern 4 + 5 → safe last
Pattern 4 (rAF chunked render) becomes relevant for the initial render path once Fix C means the filter path no longer re-renders. Pattern 5 (Intersection Observer) touches the CAA/EAA initialisation path. Both are independent of everything above and add no risk to the already-stabilised filter pipeline.

Summary

Next:  Abort token                           ← no dependencies, fixes the works-page race

* Filter Performance fixes — ready to implement (analysed, approach agreed)
** analysis

The next batch of Filter Performance fixes after a previous analysis:

- Pattern 1: incremental filter — on query extension test only previous
  match set, not all rows; invalidate on sort/fetch/settings change
- Fix C: display:none instead of re-render — keep all rows in DOM,
  toggle visibility; eliminates DOM rebuild + all post-render hooks
  from filter path; bigbox rebuild becomes one-time not per-keystroke
- Pattern 4: rAF chunked render — abort token pattern; post-render
  hooks only fire for completed render not abandoned ones
- Pattern 5: Intersection Observer for CAA — lazy-load art as cells
  scroll into viewport; guard with row-count threshold setting

Please check the code against the previous findings and decide in which order we should implement these fixes

**

What the code actually shows

  Current filter path (single-table, every keystroke):
  testRowMatch(allRows)   — cached by exact query key, misses on any extension
    ↓
  cloneNode × matches     — always runs even on cache hit
  testRowMatch(clone)     — applies highlights (mutates DOM on clone)
  renderFinalTable()      — tbody.innerHTML = '' + re-insert clones
  initCollapsableColumns  — now fast after v9.99.626, but still runs
  initCaaPics()           — recreates _caaQueue fresh (abandoned tasks keep running!)
  initEaaPics / Inline    — re-enqueues all visible art cells
  initExpandRGsFeature    — rewires ERG buttons
  initBarcodeHighlight    — scans all rows
  initRelationshipsColumn — re-populates rel cells

  The cache (_filterResultCache) only skips step 1. Steps 2–end run unconditionally every keystroke, including the _caaQueue recreation (old queued requests are abandoned but not cancelled — they keep running in parallel with the new queue).

  renderRowsChunked only triggers at ≥1000 rows (sa_chunked_render_threshold). Typical filter results (<1000 rows) take the fast synchronous path — so Pattern 4 (rAF) only touches initial load, not the filter path at all.

  No IntersectionObserver anywhere. initCaaPics eagerly enqueues every visible art anchor on every call.

  ---
  Dependency map

  Pattern 1 (incremental)  — independent; benefits filter path NOW and after Fix C
  Pattern 4 (rAF)          — independent; only affects initial chunked render path
  Fix C    (display:none)  — eliminates cloneNode + all post-render hooks from filter
  Pattern 5 (IO for CAA)   — maximally useful AFTER Fix C (initCaaPics becomes one-time)

  ---
  Recommended order

  1. Pattern 1 — implement now

  The _filterResultCache cache hit skips testRowMatch on source rows, but cloneNode + highlight application + the full render + hook chain still fire. The first time the user types "cook" character-by-character: four full O(8100) testRowMatch scans run (one per distinct key "c",
  "co", "coo", "cook"). Incremental narrowing reduces those to: O(8100) + O(matches_c) + O(matches_co) + O(matches_coo).

  Confined to runFilter(): add _lastSingleFilterKey (the previous query string + flags as a simple string) + _lastSingleMatchSet (the previous _matchingSrc array). When the new globalQuery starts with the previous and no flags changed (not regex, not exclude, no column filter
  active), run testRowMatch only on _lastSingleMatchSet. Invalidate on: sort, new fetch, settings change, column filter change, regex/exclude toggle. Falls back to full scan otherwise.

  2. Pattern 4 — pair in the same session as Pattern 1

  Trivial: replace await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0)) with an rAF-based yield inside renderRowsChunked. Only affects initial render of 8100 rows (17 chunks). The filter path takes the fast non-chunked path for typical result counts. Low risk, correct behaviour
  (guarantees a paint between chunks).

  3. Fix C — plan as its own session

  This is the architectural change. The core problem: allRows are detached <tr> elements; DOM holds clones. Fix C requires DOM rows to be the same objects as allRows (or a stable one-to-one map). The re-render path vanishes from filter; the entire hook chain (ERG, CAA,
  collapsable) runs once on initial load. Filter becomes: removeHighlights(tr) → testRowMatch(tr) → tr.style.display. Sort stays the same (already reorders DOM rows).

  The main things to plan before implementing: (a) initial render inserts source rows directly without clone-at-filter, (b) removeHighlights() strips all mb-*-filter-highlight spans before each filter pass, (c) initCollapsableColumns and initCaaPics become one-time
  post-initial-render calls, not repeated per filter.

  4. Pattern 5 — implement after Fix C

  With the current architecture initCaaPics recreates _caaQueue per filter keystroke — IntersectionObserver would be re-created each time too, negating the benefit. After Fix C, initCaaPics runs once; the observer persists for the table lifetime. Art cells that scroll into view
  trigger load lazily. Add sa_caa_io_threshold setting (e.g. 500 rows) to keep eager-load for small tables.

  ---
  Summary

  ┌─────┬─────────────────────────┬─────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────┐
  │  #  │           Fix           │ Effort  │                      Benefit                       │     When     │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────┼─────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ 1   │ Pattern 1 (incremental) │ Low     │ Cuts O(8100) scan to O(prev_matches) per extension │ Now          │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────┼─────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ 2   │ Pattern 4 (rAF)         │ Trivial │ Correct chunked render behaviour                   │ Same session │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────┼─────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ 3   │ Fix C (display:none)    │ High    │ Eliminates render + all hooks from filter path     │ Own session  │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────┼─────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ 4   │ Pattern 5 (IO CAA)      │ Medium  │ Lazy art load; maximally effective after Fix C     │ After Fix C  │
  └─────┴─────────────────────────┴─────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┘

Here's the article blurb, grouped by theme and written in plain language:

  ---
  Some updates since the initial release:

  - Added support for Ratings pages — your /user/<name>/ratings pages (and per-entity variants like /ratings/recording) now load all entries at once with full filtering and sorting, including the editor name,
  entity type, and star rating columns
  - Added support for entity-level Ratings pages — the /work/<mbid>/ratings and similar pages that list everyone who rated a specific entity are now supported as well
  - Event columns got smarter — event entries now split out separate columns for Event Type, Event Country, and Additional Info, making it much easier to filter and sort large event lists
  - Relationship icons now show rich tooltips — hovering over a relationship icon displays a proper popup with the full relationship details, highlighted to match your active filter
  - Relationship icons highlight when your filter matches — if your filter finds a row because of something in the Relationships column, the specific matching icons are outlined in red so you can see exactly
  why the row matched
  - Collapsed artwork cells show a "hidden match" hint — if a row is hidden inside a collapsed cover-art stripe but matches your filter, the expand button turns yellow with a red marker so you know there's a
  match inside
  - Status bar completely redesigned — the progress line at the top now has separate segments for cover art loading, relationship loading, and general info, each with its own hover tooltip showing detailed
  timing and counts
  - Auto-resize columns got a progress overlay — when the script measures and fits column widths on large tables, it now shows a progress overlay with elapsed time and an estimated time remaining instead of
  just freezing the page
  - Filtering is significantly faster on large tables — several rounds of optimisation (caching, smarter matching order, adaptive typing delays) cut filter response times noticeably on tables with thousands of
  rows
  - Keyboard shortcuts overhauled — shortcuts are now suppressed while you're typing in a search or filter field; the barcode highlight shortcut (Ctrl+B) and the help shortcut (Ctrl+K) are configurable in
  settings
  - IndexedDB cache statistics added to the Stats panel — shows how many relationship records are stored locally, how much space they use, and when they were last accessed
  - Sort by text length — Alt+clicking a sort arrow now sorts that column by the length of each cell's text, useful for spotting unusually long or short values
  - Alternating shade banding (the subtle colour striping that shows where sorted values change) now also works when sorting by a single column, not just multi-column sorts
  - Column resize is much more reliable — a run of fixes addressed resize minimum creep, line breaks appearing in disambiguation comments during resize, and incorrect widths on initially-collapsed sub-tables
  - Cover-art thumbnails load in a smarter order — inline thumbnails in the title column are now fetched before the smaller icons in the CAA/EAA columns, so the most visible images appear first

# [VZ: MusicBrainz - Show All Entity Data In A Consolidated View With Filtering And Multi-Sorting Capabilities](https://github.com/vzell/mb-userscripts/tree/master?tab=readme-ov-file#mb_show_all_entity_data)

## Changes since last version

### Enhancements

 * **Keyboard shortcuts** completely reworked --- direct Ctrl+ shortcuts are now disabled by default to avoid accidentally hijacking browser or OS key combinations. All actions are instead available through the Ctrl+M prefix menu: press Ctrl+M followed by a single letter to trigger any action. The prefix tooltip lists everything available. For users who prefer direct shortcuts, the old behaviour can be re-enabled in settings. The shortcuts for the keyboard help overlay and barcode highlight are now configurable.
 * **Rendering** doesn't show the "Page unresponsive" dialog anymore on large tables
 * **Auto-resize** columns got a progress overlay and is much faster on large tables --- when the script measures and fits column widths on large tables, it now shows a progress overlay with elapsed time and an estimated time remaining instead of just freezing the page (e.g. x15 on a 8100 rows table https://musicbrainz.org/artist/70248960-cb53-4ea4-943a-edb18f7d336f/releases )
 * **Filtering** is significantly faster on large tables --- several rounds of optimisation (caching, smarter matching order, adaptive typing delays) cut filter response times noticeably on tables with thousands of rows
 * **Status bar** completely redesigned --- the progress line at the top now has separate segments for cover art loading, relationship loading, and general info, each with its own hover tooltip showing detailed timing and counts
 * **Alternating shade banding** (the subtle colour striping that shows where sorted values change) now also works when *sorting by a single column*, not just multi-column sorts
 * **Cover-art thumbnails** load in a smarter order --- inline thumbnails in the title column are now fetched before the smaller icons in the CAA/EAA columns, so the most visible images appear first
 * **Collapsed artwork** cells show a "hidden match" hint --- if a row is hidden inside a collapsed cover-art stripe but matches your filter, the expand button turns yellow with a red marker so you know there's a match inside
 * **Sort by text length** --- Alt+clicking a sort arrow now sorts that column by the length of each cell's text, useful for spotting unusually long or short values
 * **Event columns** got smarter --- event entries now split out separate columns for Event Type, Event Country, and Additional Info, making it much easier to filter and sort large event lists
 * **Relationship icons** now show *rich tooltips* --- hovering over a relationship icon displays a proper popup with the full relationship details, highlighted to match your active filter
 * **Relationship icons** *highlight* when your filter matches --- if your filter finds a row because of something in the Relationships column, the specific matching icons are outlined in red so you can see exactly why the row matched
 * **IndexedDB cache statistics** added to the Stats panel --- shows how many relationship records are stored locally, how much space they use, and when they were last accessed
 * Added support for **Ratings pages** --- your /user//ratings pages (and per-entity variants like /ratings/recording) now load all entries at once with full filtering and sorting, including the editor name, entity type, and star rating columns
 * Added support for **entity-level Ratings pages** --- the /work//ratings and similar pages that list everyone who rated a specific entity are now supported as well

 ### Fixes

 * **"Save to disk"** now preserves the correct column headers when saving at the large-table render-threshold prompt --- previously the saved file could contain the wrong header names
 * **Column resize** is much more reliable --- a run of fixes addressed resize minimum creep, line breaks appearing in disambiguation comments during resize, and incorrect widths on initially-collapsed sub-tables

#+begin_example
● I've drafted the forum post covering everything from 9.99.675 through the current 9.99.746, and appended it to debug/forum.org (it's gitignored, so nothing to commit). Here it is:

  ---
  VZ: MusicBrainz - Show All Entity Data In A Consolidated View With Filtering And Multi-Sorting Capabilities

  Changes since last version

  New pages supported

  - Report pages — the full /reports index (all 117 reports, in 14 categories) and every individual report page now load, filter and sort like every other page this script handles, including inline cover-art thumbnails where a report lists releases or events, and extra date/time
  and text-length columns on reports that have a "Last edited" or "Annotation" column.
  - Your Applications page — /account/applications (your OAuth2 authorized apps, and any apps you've registered as a developer) is now consolidated into one filterable table.
  - Edit-listing pages — a big one: search results for edits, edits on a specific entity, subscribed edits, your own edits (open or all), and the "recent notes left on your edits" page are all now supported. Each edit becomes a proper table row, edit type and open/closed state
  get a colour (matching the well-known "Colourful Edits" userscript's palette, even if you don't have it installed), old/new value changes are colour-coded, and long edit details/notes can be collapsed. Edits tied to a specific release also get a small cover-art thumbnail.
  - Auto-editor elections — both the /elections overview and individual election pages.
  - Genre list, Instrument list, Edit Types documentation, and CD stub pages — /genres, /instruments, /doc/Edit_Types, and both the CD stub browsing list and individual CD stub pages all get the same filtering/sorting treatment.
  - Privileged user accounts — the /privileged page listing auto-editors, relationship editors, bots, and other special account types.
  - musicbrainz.eu mirror — the script now works there too, not just musicbrainz.org.

  Enhancements

  - Filter dropdown multi-select — the little 📊 dropdown that lists every value in a column now lets you tick several values at once instead of only picking one.
  - Collapsible long-text columns — free-text columns like "Annotation" can now be collapsed behind a "show more/less" toggle instead of stretching the row, with a configurable preview height. Wiki-style sub-headings inside an annotation stay individually collapsible too, with
  their own colour setting.
  - Auto-expand annotations on entity pages — optionally, a long native Annotation on an entity's own page can now expand automatically instead of needing an extra click (off by default).
  - Smarter Location/Area columns — the "Area" columns now split more usefully into a Locality (city) and Region (state/county) part instead of one combined value, and play nicer with popular flag-icon userscripts (Canadian Province Flags, More Flags Everywhere, etc.).
  - Optional flag icons in the filter dropdown — Country/Area/Location-style columns can now optionally show the same little flag icon in the filter dropdown as in the table itself (off by default).

  Fixes

  - Sorting no longer gets confused by hidden cover-art/event-art markers, so tables with inline thumbnails sort correctly again.
  - Sorting now applies consistently across every row of a merged release-group discography view, instead of only part of it.
  - Several rendering glitches on report pages are fixed (missing section headings, broken formatting when an annotation contained wiki-style headings, wrong or missing cover-art icons).
  - Column filtering on edit-listing pages no longer highlights the wrong column.
  - A handful of small bugs in the collapsible-column toggles are fixed (wrong item counts, a toggle that stopped responding after being clicked once).
  - Several dialogs (Settings, Save/Load to Disk, Statistics, Export, and others) now display correctly on the Applications page, which previously showed them broken/unstyled due to MusicBrainz applying stricter security rules there.
  - Minor: column headers starting with a number (e.g. "1st seconder" on election pages) no longer render with the digit stripped off.
  - Minor: fixed a column-alignment issue on pages when also using the "MusicBrainz Nuclear Tags" userscript.
#+end_example

    const REMOTE_CHANGELOG_URL = REMOTE_BASE + SCRIPT_BASE_NAME + '_CHANGELOG.json';
    const REMOTE_CACHE_TTL_MS  = 60 * 60 * 1000; // 1 hour
    const CACHE_KEY_HELP       = SCRIPT_BASE_NAME.toLowerCase() + '-remote-help-text';

* SpringsteenCoverArtUploader
** DONE CoverArtUploader
*** AI

#+begin_example
Done. Here's what was created:

  CoverArtUpload/CoverArtUpload.user.js (v1.00.001+2026-06-19) — a self-contained Tampermonkey script that:

  1. On /release/*/cover-art: Calls the MB Web Service API to find external URL relationships. For each SpringsteenLyrics.com or Jungleland.it link, injects an upload button into #content > .buttons. Button
  click fetches the external page via GM.xmlHttpRequest (CORS-free), extracts full-size image URLs, saves a queue to GM storage, then navigates to /add-cover-art.
  2. On /release/*/add-cover-art: Reads the stored queue, downloads each image as a blob, simulates a drag-and-drop onto #drop-zone (matching how ecau.js works), then sets cover-art type checkboxes and
  comments. Queue is cleared immediately on read to avoid re-triggering on reload.

  Site-specific extraction:
  - SpringsteenLyrics: finds <a target="_blank" href="*.jpg"> links (the thumbnail anchors), resolves relative paths against the page URL
  - Jungleland.it: finds <a href="*.jpg"> links (excluding thumbnail paths), converts Windows backslash paths to forward slashes before URL resolution, infers MB artwork type from filename suffix
  (_front→Front, _back→Back, _booklet→Booklet, _cd→Medium)
  - CloudFlare challenge on SpringsteenLyrics triggers a user-facing alert with instructions

  CoverArtUpload/CoverArtUpload_CHANGELOG.json — initial changelog entry.

✻ Cooked for 8m 27s

※ recap: Created CoverArtUpload.user.js, a new Tampermonkey userscript that adds upload buttons on MusicBrainz cover-art pages for SpringsteenLyrics.com and Jungleland.it links. Next: install and test in
  Tampermonkey against a real MB release. (disable recaps in /config)
#+end_example

#+begin_example
Syntax is clean. Here's what was added (v1.00.002):

  dbg logger — replaces all bare console.* calls with a prefixed helper that includes console.groupCollapsed for structured data.

  gmRequest — now logs before every request (→ GET url) and after every response as a collapsed group containing: status, statusText, finalUrl, responseHeaders, and responseLength.

  fetchImagesFromProvider — the most important addition:
  - Logs entry with provider name and URL
  - Extracts and logs the actual <title> from whatever was returned
  - Logs first 1000 chars of body in two chunks (to get past any preamble)
  - Logs all four CF signals independently (hasJustAMoment, hasCfBrowserVerification, hasCfRayId, hasCfChallenge via __cf_chl_) so you can see exactly which one fired (or didn't)

  extractSpringsteenImages — logs count of a[target="_blank"] found, then a per-link breakdown table showing which of the three conditions each link passed/failed, with the actual href values marked [✓]/[✗].

  extractJunglelandImages — same per-link breakdown.

  Upload pipeline — downloadImage logs filename/size/mimeType; processUploadQueue logs queue contents, MBID comparison, and each step of drop/setParameters.

  Open the browser DevTools console when you click the button and you'll see exactly what was returned and which condition is firing.
#+end_example

#+begin_example
The logs confirm the issue: CloudFlare is returning its JS challenge page even though the user has authenticated. The problem is that GM_xmlhttpRequest — even though it shares the browser's cookie jar —
  sends the request in a way CF's bot detection catches (different TLS fingerprint, missing Sec-Fetch-* headers, etc.). The cf_clearance cookie may also be SameSite=Lax and not sent on cross-origin requests.

  The reliable fix is a popup approach: open springsteenlyrics.com in a real browser tab (so it passes CF), have the userscript running there extract the images and postMessage them back to the MB page, then
  close the popup. This works because the actual browser loads the page normally.


Here's what changed in v1.00.003:

  Root cause: GM_xmlhttpRequest fails CloudFlare's bot detection regardless of whether you have a valid cf_clearance cookie, because CF also checks the TLS fingerprint (JA3/JA4) and Sec-Fetch-* headers —
  things that differ from a real browser navigation even when cookies are present.

  Fix — popup strategy:

  1. @match added for springsteenlyrics.com — the userscript now runs there too.
  2. Provider gets usePopup: true — routes SpringsteenLyrics through the new path.
  3. fetchImagesViaPopup(url, provider, mbid) — opens a real browser popup to the springsteenlyrics URL with ?cau_extract=1&cau_mbid=MBID appended. Waits up to 30 s for a postMessage from that popup, then
  closes it. If the popup is blocked, gives a clear error.
  4. runAsSpringsteenPopup() — runs on springsteenlyrics.com when cau_extract is in the URL. Reads images directly from the live DOM (no refetch needed — the browser already loaded the page normally, CF
  already passed), then calls window.opener.postMessage({ type: 'cau_images', images }, 'https://musicbrainz.org') and closes itself after 1.2 s.

  The popup is visible briefly so the user can see it worked; if CF does show a challenge inside the popup the user can solve it there, after which they'd need to click the button again (the 30 s timeout will
  have fired).

  recaps in /config)
#+end_example

Everything looks correct. Here's what changed in v1.00.004:

  Root cause confirmed by the log: mimeType="text/html" size=6041 on every .jpg fetch — GM_xmlhttpRequest from the MusicBrainz origin was hitting CloudFlare and receiving its ~6 KB challenge page instead of
  the actual JPEG, for every image file, even after the HTML-extraction popup worked.

  Fix — three-part:

  1. runAsSpringsteenPopup() — after extracting the 6 image URLs from the live DOM, it now calls fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' }) for each one in parallel. This runs inside the springsteenlyrics.com
  popup context where the CF session is valid, so the browser delivers real JPEG data. Each blob is converted to a base64 data URL via FileReader and included as a dataUrl field in the postMessage payload.
  2. dataUrlToFile() (new helper) — decodes a data URL back into a File object on the MusicBrainz side.
  3. processUploadQueue() — checks image.dataUrl; if present, calls dataUrlToFile() instead of downloadImage(). The downloadImage() / GM_xmlhttpRequest path is still used as a fallback for Jungleland.it (no
  CF) and for any popup fetch that fails individually.

  The popup will now stay open for a few extra seconds while it downloads all images before posting — that's expected. The 120-second timeout gives plenty of headroom for slow connections.

#+begin_example
he difference is structural, not a bug. The two providers use fundamentally different code paths:

SpringsteenLyrics — all the real work (HTML fetch, image extraction, per-image binary fetch) happens inside the popup window. The MB page only ever sees the final postMessage. Its console shows one compact
line:
fetchImagesViaPopup: postMessage received {type: 'cau_images', images: Array(6)}
The detailed per-image logs are in the popup's DevTools console, not the release page's.

Jungleland — everything runs inline in run() on the MB page. Every gmRequest call, every extractor step, every gmFetchDataUrl call is logged directly to the release page's console, so you see the full trace.

The logs will always look different because the popup strategy intentionally moves execution to another window. There's no way to make them symmetric without either:
- Logging inside the popup and somehow relaying those messages back (needless complexity), or
- Dropping the popup for SpringsteenLyrics too (not possible due to CloudFlare).

The important thing from jungland.debug is that Jungleland is now working — the last two lines confirm it:

[ArtStation #250] object URL renders OK: prov-…-1.jpg image/jpeg 385824B 1181×929
Both images fetched, converted to dataUrl, and rendered correctly in ArtStation.
#+end_example

#+begin_example
  The bug is in ArtStation's wire() function (line 738-754). It runs before hydrateImgs() and does th.querySelector('img') on every .as-thumb. For Jungleland new items, the only img inside .as-thumb
  at that point is the provider badge favicon (as-prov img), not the gallery image (which hasn't been inserted yet). wire() misassigns the gallery-image error handler to the favicon. When
  https://www.jungleland.it/favicon.ico fails to load (404 or blocked), that handler fires → th.classList.add('na') (without as-na-new) → .as-thumb.na img { display:none } hides all imgs including the gallery
  JPEG → "Not on the Cover Art Archive yet" appears.

  Local drag-drop has no provider badge so th.querySelector('img') returns null and the handler is never assigned. SpringsteenLyrics' favicon loads (CF allows it), so the handler is assigned but never
  triggers.

  Fix: remove the icon property from the Jungleland provider so no <img> appears in .as-thumb before hydrateImgs() runs.

● The root cause is confirmed. thumbImg() for _new items returns an <span class="as-imghost"> placeholder (not an <img>), but the provider badge <span class="as-prov"><img src="favicon.ico"></span> IS inside
  .as-thumb. When wire() runs before hydrateImgs(), th.querySelector('img') grabs the favicon — the only img there — and assigns the gallery-image onerror to it. When https://www.jungleland.it/favicon.ico
  fails (404), that handler fires th.classList.add('na') (no as-na-new), and .as-thumb.na img { display:none } hides the gallery JPEG that hydrateImgs() later inserts. SpringsteenLyrics escapes only because

● Root cause summary:

  ArtStation's wire() runs before hydrateImgs() in every render() call. It does th.querySelector('img') on each .as-thumb to find the gallery image — but for _new items, thumbImg() emits an <span
  class="as-imghost"> placeholder, not an <img>. The only <img> present in .as-thumb before hydrateImgs() is the provider badge favicon (<span class="as-prov"><img src="favicon.ico"></span>). wire() misassigns
  the gallery-image onerror to that favicon. When https://www.jungleland.it/favicon.ico 404s, the handler fires th.classList.add('na'), and the CSS rule .as-thumb.na img { display:none } hides the gallery
  JPEG that hydrateImgs() subsequently inserts. SpringsteenLyrics escaped only because its favicon loads successfully through CloudFlare.

  Fix: remove the icon property from the Jungleland provider so no <img> appears in .as-thumb before hydrateImgs() runs.

  ├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Logo                │ ['Logo']                                          │ —                                                                                                                │
  ├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ anything else       │ []                                                │ —                                                                                                                │
  └─────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  The Wristband grouping rule is the key design decision: GA_Sun_Pass → runs of non-caps qualifiers after each all-caps zone token are space-joined into one phrase, giving wristband, GA, sun pass rather than
  wristband, GA, sun, pass.
#+end_example

*** download ZIP

Is it possible to additionally download all images into a ZIP file to the local machine ?
Do not implement yet

● Yes, straightforward. The two pieces needed are both already available in the browser:

   1. The image bytes — the popup already fetches every image as a dataUrl before postMessage-ing them back. Those data URLs can be decoded back to binary without any extra network requests.
   2. ZIP creation — the browser has no native ZIP API, but fflate (https://github.com/101arrowz/fflate) (a small, zero-dependency library, ~30 KB) can be loaded via a @require in the userscript header and used
      to build a ZIP in memory, then trigger a download via a synthetic <a download> click. ArtStation itself already uses this pattern for its bulk download feature (dlZip in art_station.user.js, lines 737–740).

      The simplest approach would be a second return path in the SpringsteenLyrics run(): instead of (or alongside) handing blobs to ArtStation, decode the data URLs into Uint8Arrays, pass them to fflate.zip(),
      and trigger a <a href="blob:…" download="springsteen-artwork.zip"> click. No server, no extra permissions needed beyond what's already granted.

      Just say the word when you want it implemented.

*** resize images

Is it possible for the springsteenlyrics provider to resize images before handing over to ArtStation, when the image dimensions are bigger than some threshold.
Do not implement yet.

#+begin_example
● Yes, it's feasible. The popup already has the full image as a dataUrl before postMessageing it back, so it can draw into an offscreen <canvas>, check img.naturalWidth/naturalHeight against a threshold, scale
  down, and call canvas.toDataURL('image/jpeg', quality) — all before the postMessage. The logic would live in runAsSpringsteenPopup, extending the existing per-image fetch loop.

  The main tradeoff to be aware of: re-encoding JPEG→canvas→JPEG is lossy regardless of quality setting, and PNG→canvas→JPEG changes format. If the original is already below the threshold it passes through
  untouched, but anything resized loses a generation. MusicBrainz's CAA does accept large originals and serves its own scaled versions to consumers, so the question worth settling before implementing is: what
  threshold actually matters (e.g. longest edge > 3000 px? file size > N MB?) and whether re-encode quality loss is acceptable for images above it.
#+end_example
